_about: A short guide to how types and prophecies work, written for this app. Catechism and Council numbers are pointers; check them against the text.

entries.title: One story, read at more than one level
entries.note: The Church reads every passage first for what its human author meant (the literal sense), because the other senses are built on it. On that foundation it recognises three spiritual senses: the allegorical (how events point to Christ), the moral (how they teach us to live) and the anagogical (how they point to our end in heaven). Types belong to the allegorical sense.

entries.title: A type is a person, place or event that points forward
entries.note: Adam, the Passover lamb, the manna, the temple and the exodus are real people, places and events with their own meaning. Christian writers, beginning with the New Testament itself, saw in them a pattern that Christ completes, and the fulfilment is always greater than the shadow. Augustine's phrase, repeated at the Council, is that the New Testament lies hidden in the Old and the Old is made plain in the New.

entries.title: Prophecy is more than prediction
entries.note: Prophets speak first to their own people and time. The New Testament uses their words in several ways: a plain promise that is kept (a ruler from Bethlehem, Micah 5), a pattern that is repeated (Israel called out of Egypt, Hosea 11, and Jesus called out of Egypt), and words that have a nearer and a further sense (the sign of Emmanuel, Isaiah 7). Reading each case on its own terms is more honest than treating every quotation as a forecast.

entries.title: The Jewish world of the first century
entries.note: The first Christians were Jews who read Scripture in the synagogue and Temple. The ancient rabbinic writings applied hundreds of Old Testament passages to the Messiah, as the appendix to Edersheim's Life and Times (in the library) shows from the sources. That helps explain why the Gospel writers could assume readers would hear an echo. Modern Catholic scholars such as Brant Pitre work in this area; their books are copyrighted, so the app links to them and does not copy them.

entries.title: How to spot a real type
entries.note: A responsible typology has a check: the New Testament itself names the correspondence (Adam, the bronze serpent, Jonah, Melchizedek), or the Church's liturgy and the Fathers have received it as a pattern (the Red Sea and baptism). Resemblances that nobody in the tradition has drawn are interesting guesses, not teaching. The notes in this app say which kind each one is.

entries.title: Where you meet typology at Mass
entries.note: The Easter Vigil readings (creation, Abraham and Isaac, the Red Sea) are chosen as types of Christ's passover. The Exsultet sings the Passover night as Christ's. Ordinary Time pairs an Old Testament reading with the Gospel because the two answer each other.
